subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview:
In this unit you will learn what a half is. You will see that a whole can be split into parts, that halves must be two equal parts, and how to make halves by folding and by drawing a line. You will find that halves can look different but still be halves, and that two halves put back together make one whole.

What you will need: paper shapes to fold and cut: circles, squares, rectangles and triangles (draw and cut a few from scrap paper) safety scissors (used with adult help) and a pencil or crayon.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: Understand that a half is one of two equal parts of a whole.
Recognise when a shape or object is divided into halves.
Divide simple shapes into halves by drawing a line.
Tell the difference between equal and unequal parts.
Know that two halves make a whole.
Complete the other half of a shape to make a whole.
Find and use halves in everyday life, such as sharing food fairly.

concepts.title: A Whole and Its Parts
concepts.explanation: Before you can understand a half, you need the words whole and part. Start with something complete — a whole anjero, a whole mango, a whole biscuit — and name it clearly as ‘the whole’. Then break or cut it and talk about the parts you have made. Keep the language simple and repeat it often across the week.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Hold up a whole anjero. Say, ‘This is the whole anjero.’ Now tear it into two pieces and say, ‘Now I have two parts.’ At this first stage do not worry whether the parts are equal — the aim is simply that the child hears and uses ‘whole’ and ‘part’. Let the child tear their own paper shape and tell you how many parts they made.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look — this is a whole date. One whole date.” You: “Now I break it. How many parts do I have now?” Child: “Two!” You: “Yes. Two parts. Soon we will make the two parts fair and equal.”

concepts.title: Equal Parts vs Unequal Parts
concepts.explanation: This is the single most important idea in the unit: a half is not just any piece — it must be one of two equal parts. It is easy to think that any two pieces are ‘halves’. The way in is fair sharing, something every child feels strongly about. If one child gets a big piece and the other a small piece, that is not fair, and it is not halves.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Break a date or biscuit into one big piece and one small piece. Offer the child the small piece and ask, ‘Is this fair? Do we both have the same?’ The child will quickly say no. Then split a second date into two equal pieces and ask again. Draw out the word equal — ‘the same size’ — and its opposite unequal. Put an equal example and an unequal example side by side so the difference is easy to see. A powerful check for ‘equal’ is to fold and match. Fold a paper shape so the two parts sit exactly on top of each other; if the edges match perfectly, the parts are equal and you have made halves. If the edges do not match, the parts are unequal. Let the child do the folding and feel for themselves when the edges line up. This physical test is far more convincing to a five-year-old than simply looking.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “I will share this anjero. Here is your piece.” (give the small one) Child: “That is not fair — yours is bigger!” You: “You are right! These parts are unequal. Halves must be equal — the same for both of us. Let us cut it fairly.”

concepts.title: Making Halves by Folding and Drawing
concepts.explanation: Once you can spot equal parts, you are ready to make halves themselves. Folding comes first because the paper does the ‘measuring’ for you — when the edges match, the fold line shows a true half. Drawing a line comes next, and is harder, so be patient with wobbly lines. Fold a paper circle so the two sides match exactly, then open it out and trace the fold line — that line splits the circle into two halves. Try it with a square and a rectangle before moving on to drawing the line yourself.
concepts.example: An important discovery is that a shape can be halved in more than one way. A square can be folded top-to-bottom, side-to-side, or corner-to-corner — and every one of those gives two equal halves. Try two or three different fold lines on identical squares so you see that halves do not have to look the same, as long as the two parts are equal. A circle is especially rich here: any straight line through its centre makes two halves, so there are endless ways to do it.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Give the child a paper circle. Ask them to fold it so ‘the two sides match exactly’. Open it up and trace the fold line together — ‘this line splits the circle into two halves’. Repeat with a square and a rectangle. Then move to drawing: on a fresh shape, draw a straight line ‘down the middle’ to make two equal parts. A folded shape beside them gives a helpful guide.

concepts.title: Halves Can Be Different Shapes but Equal Size
concepts.explanation: Here is a subtle idea. When you fold a square corner to corner, the two halves are triangles — they look different from the halves you get folding straight across, which are rectangles. Yet all of these are still true halves, because each is one of two equal parts. The key message: halves must be equal in size, but they do not have to be the same shape as some other way of halving.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Fold one square straight across and one square corner to corner. Lay the two triangles on top of each other to show they match — equal. Then talk about how a straight fold gives two rectangle halves and a diagonal fold gives two triangle halves. Both are correct. This prevents the common belief that only one ‘proper’ way of cutting counts as halving.

concepts.title: Two Halves Make a Whole
concepts.explanation: The final idea completes the circle: if you put the two halves back together, you get the whole again. This is what makes a half a half — two of them rebuild the original. It also quietly plants the seed that fractions are parts that add back up to one whole, an idea you will meet properly in later years.
concepts.example: Confusing ‘half of one thing’ with ‘one of two things’. Half of a single mango is one of its two equal parts. Later years cover half of a group; keep this unit to halving one whole object or shape.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: After cutting a paper shape into two halves, slide them back together to remake the whole. Say the words as they do it: ‘two halves… make one whole’. Play matching games where the child pairs a half-shape with its partner to build a complete shape. The ‘Complete the Other Half’ drawing activity — where you draw the missing half of a butterfly, a house or a face — is another lovely way to feel that two halves make a whole. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “You cut the circle into two halves. Now push them back together.” Child: (slides the pieces together) You: “Look! Two halves make one whole circle again. Two halves make a whole.” Thinking any two pieces are halves. If a whole is cut into a big piece and a small piece, you may still call them halves. Return to fair sharing and the fold-and-match test — halves must be equal. Believing halves must be the same shape. A diagonal fold makes triangle halves; a straight fold makes rectangle halves. Both are correct. Halves must be equal in size, not identical in shape. Thinking a shape can only be halved one way. Show several different fold lines on identical squares and circles so you see there are many ways.

explorations.title: A Whole and Its Parts
explorations.context: Before you can understand a half, you need the words whole and part. Start with something complete — a whole anjero, a whole mango, a whole biscuit — and name it clearly as ‘the whole’. Then break or cut it and talk about the parts you have made.
explorations.prompt: You break a whole biscuit into two pieces. What do we call the complete biscuit before you broke it?
explorations.hint: Think of the word for something complete, before it is split into parts.
explorations.explanation: At this early stage the goal is simply for you to use the words ‘whole’ and ‘part’ confidently, before worrying about whether the parts are equal — that idea comes in the next lesson. Naming a whole object clearly before breaking it gives you something concrete to compare the resulting pieces against.

explorations.title: Equal Parts vs Unequal Parts
explorations.context: This is the single most important idea in the unit: a half is not just any piece — it must be one of two equal parts. It is easy to think that any two pieces are ‘halves’. The way in is fair sharing, something every child feels strongly about.
explorations.prompt: A biscuit is broken into one big piece and one tiny piece. Are these two pieces equal or unequal?
explorations.hint: Compare the two pieces side by side - do they match in size?
explorations.explanation: Your sense of fairness is the fastest route into ‘equal’: if a sharing feels unfair, the pieces are not halves. Once you reject the unequal split, check for equal parts properly, by holding the pieces side by side or stacking one on top of the other.

explorations.title: Making Halves by Folding and Drawing
explorations.context: Once you can spot equal parts, you are ready to make halves themselves. Folding comes first because the paper does the ‘measuring’ for you — when the edges match, the fold line shows a true half.
explorations.prompt: You fold a paper circle so both sides match exactly, then open it up again. What has your fold made?
explorations.hint: Look at the line left by the fold - does it split the circle into two matching parts?
explorations.explanation: Folding lets the paper prove the two parts are equal, since edges that do not match show up immediately — this is why folding should always come before drawing a line freehand. Once the fold line is opened and traced, you have a real line to copy when you later try drawing a half without folding first.

explorations.title: Halves Can Be Different Shapes but Equal Size
explorations.context: Here is a subtle idea worth handling gently. When you fold a square corner to corner, the two halves are triangles — they look different from the halves you get folding straight across, which are rectangles.
explorations.prompt: One square is folded straight across to make two rectangles. An identical square is folded corner to corner to make two triangles. Are both pairs still true halves?
explorations.hint: Halves must be equal in size - they do not have to be the same shape as each other.
explorations.explanation: Laying the two triangles from a corner-to-corner fold on top of the two rectangles from a straight-across fold shows they are not the same shape, even though both pairs are true halves. The message to repeat is that halves must match each other in size, not in shape — a square can be halved in more than one way and still be halved correctly.

explorations.title: Two Halves Make a Whole
explorations.context: The final idea completes the circle: if you put the two halves back together, you get the whole again. This is what makes a half a half — two of them rebuild the original.
explorations.prompt: You cut a paper square into two equal halves, then push the two halves back together. What shape do you get?
explorations.hint: Two equal halves always fit back together to remake the shape they came from.
explorations.explanation: Sliding the two cut halves back together and watching the original shape reappear is what proves they really were equal halves in the first place — if they do not fit back into a whole, they were not true halves. Saying ‘two halves make one whole’ as the pieces are pushed together ties the words directly to the action.

explorations.title: A Whole and Its Parts
explorations.context: Before you can understand a half, you need the words whole and part. Start with something complete — a whole anjero, a whole mango, a whole biscuit — and name it clearly as ‘the whole’. Then break or cut it and talk about the parts you have made.
explorations.prompt: A circle is split by a straight line right through its centre, making two same-size pieces. What do we call these two pieces?
explorations.hint: Two equal parts of a whole are called this.
explorations.explanation: A circle split by a line straight through its centre is a clear example to return to: naming the full shape ‘the whole’ before the cut, and the two resulting pieces ‘parts’, keeps the vocabulary consistent across every shape you meet. Whether those two parts are equal is the very next question to ask once the words are secure.

methods.title: How to Show That a Half Is One of Two Equal Parts
methods.example: Example: Break one whole date into two same-size pieces — each piece is a half.
steps: Start with one whole object, such as a date or a biscuit, and say its name: 'This is the whole date.'
Break or cut the whole into two pieces that are exactly the same size.
Show the two same-size pieces side by side and say: 'These are two halves — one of two equal parts.'

methods.title: How to Spot Equal Parts vs Unequal Parts
methods.example: Example: Break a biscuit into a big piece and a small piece and ask, 'Is this fair?'
steps: Break or cut an object, such as a biscuit or an orange, into two pieces without measuring.
Hold the two pieces side by side, or stack one on top of the other, to compare their size.
If the pieces match exactly, say 'These are equal parts — halves.' If one is bigger, say 'These are unequal parts — not halves.'

methods.title: How to Fold a Shape to Make Two Halves
methods.example: Example: Fold a paper circle so the edges meet exactly, then open it to see the fold line.
steps: Take a paper shape, such as a circle or a square, cut from scrap paper.
Fold the shape so that the two sides land exactly on top of each other.
Open the shape and trace the fold line with a crayon, saying 'This line makes two halves.'

methods.title: How to Tell If a Picture Shows True Halves
methods.example: Example: Look at a square split by a line — are the two parts exactly the same size?
steps: Look carefully at the line drawn on the shape in the picture.
Compare the two parts it makes — check if they look the same size and same shape, or different.
Tick the picture only if the two parts are equal; put a cross if one part is bigger than the other.

methods.title: How to Check That Two Halves Make a Whole
methods.example: Example: Cut a paper square into two equal triangles, then slide them back together.
steps: Cut a paper shape into two halves along the fold line.
Push the two halves back together so their straight edges touch.
Check that the shape looks exactly like the whole shape you started with — if it does, the two halves make a whole.

methods.title: How to Draw the Missing Half of a Shape
methods.example: Example: One half of a circle is drawn on the page — draw the matching half to complete it.
steps: Look at the half-shape already drawn on the page and notice its outline.
Picture what the missing half must look like so both sides match exactly.
Draw the missing half so the finished shape is a whole, complete circle, square, or rectangle.

workedExamples.title: Sharing a Whole Date Into Two Halves
workedExamples.prompt: Amina has one whole date. She wants to share it fairly with her brother. How can she split it into halves?
workedExamples.solution: Amina breaks the date into two pieces. She checks that both pieces are the same size by holding them side by side. Since the two pieces are equal, each piece is a half. Now she gives one half to her brother and keeps one half for herself.

workedExamples.title: Is the Orange Split Into Halves?
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan cuts an orange into two pieces. One piece is much bigger than the other. Are these two pieces halves?
workedExamples.solution: Hassan compares the two pieces by placing them side by side. He sees that one piece is bigger and one piece is smaller, so they are not the same size. Because the parts are unequal, this cut has NOT made halves — a true half needs two equal parts.

workedExamples.title: Drawing a Line to Halve a Square
workedExamples.prompt: Layla has a paper square. She wants to draw one line so the square is split into two equal halves.
workedExamples.solution: Layla folds the square in half first so the edges match exactly. She opens it up and traces a straight line along the fold, from one edge to the opposite edge. This line splits the square into two equal halves.

workedExamples.title: Tick the Picture That Shows Halves
workedExamples.prompt: Look at two pictures of a circle. Picture A has a line straight through the middle, making two same-size pieces. Picture B has a wobbly line making one big piece and one small piece. Which picture shows halves?
workedExamples.solution: In Picture A, the two pieces are exactly the same size, so it shows halves — tick it. In Picture B, one piece is bigger than the other, so the parts are unequal and it does not show halves — put a cross.

workedExamples.title: Putting Two Halves Back Together
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf cuts a paper rectangle into two equal halves. He then pushes the two halves back together. What shape does he get?
workedExamples.solution: Each half is exactly the same size, so when Yusuf slides the straight edges together, the two halves line up perfectly. Putting the two halves back together remakes the original whole rectangle — this shows that two halves always make one whole.

workedExamples.title: Completing the Missing Half of a Circle
workedExamples.prompt: Half of a circle is drawn on the page. Draw the other half so the shape becomes a whole circle.
workedExamples.solution: Look carefully at the curve of the drawn half. Draw a matching curve on the other side so both halves are the same size and shape. When both halves are joined, the picture becomes one complete, whole circle.

workedExamples.title: Sharing Dates Fairly Between Two Children
workedExamples.prompt: A mother has 8 dried dates and wants to share them equally between her two children so each gets a half of the dates. How many dates does each child get?
workedExamples.solution: The mother lays out all 8 dates and gives one date to each child in turn, going back and forth. When all 8 dates are given out, each child has 4 dates. Each child received half of the dates — 4 each — so the sharing is fair and equal.

workedExamples.title: Folding a Square Two Different Ways
workedExamples.prompt: Ibrahim folds a paper square straight across the middle, and his sister folds an identical square corner to corner. Do both children still make halves?
workedExamples.solution: Ibrahim's fold gives two equal rectangles. His sister's fold gives two equal triangles. The shapes look different, but each half is still one of two equal parts of the same whole square, so both children have correctly made halves.

workedExamples.title: Drawing a Line to Halve a Rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: Fatima has a paper rectangle. Show her how to draw one straight line so the rectangle is split into two equal halves.
workedExamples.solution: Fatima folds the rectangle so the short ends meet exactly, checking the edges line up. She opens the rectangle and draws a straight line along the fold crease. This line splits the rectangle into two equal halves, each the same size and shape.

workedExamples.title: Finding a Second Way to Halve a Square
workedExamples.prompt: A square has already been folded straight across to make two halves. Can it be folded a different way and still make two equal halves?
workedExamples.solution: Yes. The same square can also be folded corner to corner. This makes two equal triangles instead of two equal rectangles. Both ways give two equal parts of the same whole square, so both are true halves — just a different shape of half.

workedExamples.title: Checking a Halved Rectangle by Folding
workedExamples.prompt: Draw one line across a rectangle to split it into two equal halves, then check your line is correct.
workedExamples.solution: Draw a straight line down the middle of the rectangle, from one long edge to the other. Fold the rectangle along your line. If the two sides match exactly with no overlap or gap, the line has made two true, equal halves.

workedExamples.title: Colouring Half of a Shape
workedExamples.prompt: A square is split into two equal parts by a line. Colour in just one half of the square, no more and no less.
workedExamples.solution: First find the line that splits the square into two equal parts. Choose one side of the line and colour only that part all the way to the edges. Leave the other equal part uncoloured, so exactly one half of the square is coloured.

practice.prompt: Kaltun has one whole mango. She cuts it into two equal pieces. What do we call each piece?
practice.answer: Each piece is called a half — one of two equal parts of the whole mango.
practice.hint: Remember: a half is one of two EQUAL parts of a whole.

practice.prompt: Look at a circle cut straight through the middle into two same-size pieces. Are the two pieces halves?
practice.answer: Yes, because the two pieces are exactly the same size — that makes them halves.
practice.hint: Check if the two parts are exactly the same size before calling them halves.

practice.prompt: Fold a paper square so both sides match exactly. What has your fold made?
practice.answer: The fold has split the square into two equal halves.
practice.hint: A good fold makes the two sides land exactly on top of each other.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is split by a line into one big part and one small part. Is this rectangle split into halves?
practice.answer: No — the two parts are unequal (one is bigger than the other), so this is not split into halves.
practice.hint: Halves must be the same size. Compare the two parts carefully.

practice.prompt: A triangle shape is split by a line into two parts that match exactly when folded together. Tick or cross: are these two parts equal?
practice.answer: Tick — the two parts are equal because they match exactly when folded together.
practice.hint: If the parts match perfectly when folded, they are equal.

practice.prompt: A circle is split down the middle by a straight line through its centre, making two same-size pieces. What are these two pieces called?
practice.answer: They are called halves, because they are two equal parts of the whole circle.
practice.hint: A line through the very centre of a circle makes two equal halves.

practice.prompt: A square is cut into one big part and one small part. Can we call the small part a half? Why or why not?
practice.answer: No, we cannot call it a half, because the two parts are not the same size — a half must be one of two EQUAL parts.
practice.hint: A half can never be smaller or bigger than the other part — they must match.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is split across the middle into two same-size strips. Are the two strips halves? How do you know?
practice.answer: Yes, the two strips are halves, because they are exactly the same size — two equal parts of the whole rectangle.
practice.hint: Compare the width and length of both strips to check they match.

practice.prompt: Draw one straight line across a square so that it makes two equal halves.
practice.answer: Draw the line straight through the middle, from one edge to the opposite edge, so both parts are exactly the same size.
practice.hint: Fold first to find the middle, then trace your line along the fold.

practice.prompt: ★ Draw a line from one corner of a square to the opposite corner. Are the two triangles you made equal halves?
practice.answer: Yes — the two triangles are exactly the same size, so they are true halves, even though they are triangles and not rectangles.
practice.hint: Halves can be a different shape from other halves, as long as they are equal in size.

practice.prompt: ★ A rectangle is folded corner to corner instead of straight across. Does this fold still make two equal halves?
practice.answer: Yes, as long as both triangles made by the fold are exactly the same size, they are still two equal halves of the rectangle.
practice.hint: Check the two triangle pieces match exactly by laying one on top of the other.

practice.prompt: A circle is split into two equal parts. Colour exactly one half of the circle red.
practice.answer: Colour only one of the two equal parts red, leaving the other equal part uncoloured — that is exactly one half of the circle.
practice.hint: Find the line that splits the circle into two equal parts before you start colouring.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

terms: The complete thing before it is split
One of two equal parts of a whole
The same size as each other
Give out fairly, the same to each
commonMistakes: A common mistake is cutting off a small piece for the brother and keeping the bigger piece
Check both pieces match in size before calling them halves — that is what makes sharing fair.
A buyer might assume any two pieces cut from one item must be 'halves.' Only equal-size pieces count as halves
An unequal cut is not a half, even if there are two pieces.
A common mistake is calling any piece of a broken biscuit 'a half' even if the pieces are different sizes
Remember: only EQUAL pieces are true halves — check the sizes match before naming them halves.

fluency.prompt: One whole biscuit is broken into two equal pieces. What is each piece called?
fluency.hint: Equal parts of a whole, and there are two of them.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is calling any piece of a broken biscuit 'a half' even if the pieces are different sizes. Remember: only EQUAL pieces are true halves — check the sizes match before naming them halves.

fluency.prompt: A biscuit is broken into one big piece and one tiny piece. Are these two pieces equal or unequal?
fluency.hint: Compare the sizes — do they match, or does one look bigger?
fluency.errorFeedback: It is easy to say 'equal' just because there are two pieces, ignoring the size difference. Put the two pieces side by side so the size gap is obvious before you answer.

fluency.prompt: You want to split a square into halves by drawing one line. Where should the line go?
fluency.answer: Straight through the middle, from one edge to the opposite edge.
fluency.hint: Fold the square first — the fold line shows you exactly where to draw.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is drawing the line near one edge instead of through the middle, which makes two unequal parts. Fold the paper first so the true middle line is easy to find.

fluency.prompt: A shape is split by a line into two parts that are the same size and shape. Do you tick it as halves, or cross it?
fluency.answer: Tick it — the two equal parts are halves.
fluency.hint: Same size and same shape means the parts are equal.
fluency.errorFeedback: It is easy to cross out a shape just because the line isn't perfectly straight, even though the two parts are still the same size. Focus on whether the SIZES match, not on how neat the line looks.

fluency.prompt: You have two halves of the same circle. If you put them back together, what do you get?
fluency.hint: Two halves always rebuild the one whole they came from.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might think joining two halves makes a bigger or different shape. Slide the two cut halves back together and you will see it makes the same whole circle again.

fluency.prompt: Half of a square is already drawn. What must you draw to complete the whole square?
fluency.answer: The matching other half, the same size and shape as the half already drawn.
fluency.hint: Look at the drawn half carefully, then copy its size on the other side.
fluency.errorFeedback: It is easy to draw a half that is too big or too small next to the first one. Check both halves match, by folding or by measuring, before you finish.

fluency.prompt: There are 6 dates to share fairly between 2 children so each gets a half. How many dates does each child get?
fluency.hint: Share the dates out one at a time, turn by turn, until none are left.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is giving one child more dates than the other because sharing wasn't done one-at-a-time. Deal the dates alternately, one to each child, so both totals stay equal.

fluency.prompt: A square folded straight across makes two rectangles. The same size square folded corner to corner makes two triangles. Are both pairs true halves?
fluency.answer: Yes — both pairs are true halves, because in each case the two parts are equal in size, even though they are different shapes.
fluency.hint: Halves must be equal in SIZE, not the same shape as other halves.
fluency.errorFeedback: It is easy to think only rectangle-shaped pieces can be 'halves' and that triangles don't count. Any two equal-size parts are halves, whatever shape they are.

fluency.prompt: Draw one line across a triangle-shaped piece of paper so it splits into two equal halves.
fluency.answer: Fold the triangle so its two sides match, then draw your line along that fold to make two equal halves.
fluency.hint: Folding first helps you find exactly where an equal line should go.
fluency.errorFeedback: Guessing a line without folding first usually makes one part bigger than the other. Always fold to find the true middle before you draw the line.

fluency.prompt: ★ Draw a line from corner to corner of a square. Do the two triangles made count as equal halves?
fluency.answer: Yes, the two corner-to-corner triangles are equal halves, as long as they are exactly the same size.
fluency.hint: Lay one triangle on top of the other to check they match exactly.
fluency.errorFeedback: You might assume a diagonal line can never make true halves, because it looks different from a straight-across line. The two triangles are still equal in size, so they are still halves.

fluency.prompt: ★ A rectangle is folded so the two short ends meet exactly. Does this fold make two equal halves?
fluency.answer: Yes — when the short ends meet exactly, the fold makes two equal halves, each half a smaller rectangle.
fluency.hint: Check that the folded edges line up all the way round with no gap.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common error is folding at an angle so the edges don't quite line up, which makes unequal parts. Straighten the fold until every edge matches before calling it a half.

fluency.prompt: A rectangle is split into two equal parts by a line. Colour exactly one of the two parts.
fluency.answer: Colour only one equal part fully, leaving the other equal part blank — that is one half of the rectangle coloured.
fluency.hint: Find the dividing line first, then colour just one side of it.
fluency.errorFeedback: It is easy to colour a bit of both parts instead of one whole part. Colour ALL the way to the edges of just one part, and leave the other part completely empty.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Maryan has one whole chapati for breakfast. She wants to share it fairly with her little brother so they each get a half. How should she cut it?
realProblems.answer: Maryan should cut the chapati into two equal pieces, checking that both pieces are the same size, so each piece is a true half.
realProblems.hint: Fold the chapati in half first to find where to cut evenly.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is cutting off a small piece for the brother and keeping the bigger piece. Check both pieces match in size before calling them halves — that is what makes sharing fair.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a trader cuts a watermelon into two pieces to sell as halves. One piece is clearly bigger than the other. Has the trader really made two halves?
realProblems.answer: No — because the two pieces are not the same size, they are unequal parts, not true halves.
realProblems.hint: Look at the two pieces side by side — do they match in size?
realProblems.errorFeedback: A buyer might assume any two pieces cut from one item must be 'halves.' Only equal-size pieces count as halves — an unequal cut is not a half, even if there are two pieces.

realProblems.prompt: On a journey, a family shares one whole loaf of bread. They fold it in half to check it is fair before breaking it. What should they check the fold for?
realProblems.answer: They should check that the two sides of the fold match exactly — if the edges line up with no part sticking out, the fold makes two true equal halves.
realProblems.hint: A good fold makes both sides land exactly on top of each other.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is folding roughly and breaking along a crooked fold, giving unequal pieces. Straighten the fold fully before breaking so both halves match.

realProblems.prompt: Every morning, two brothers share one whole orange. Today's orange is cut into two pieces — one piece has 5 segments and the other has 3 segments. Is this a fair half each?
realProblems.answer: No — since one piece has more segments (5) than the other (3), the pieces are not equal, so it is not a fair half each.
realProblems.hint: Count the segments in each piece and compare the numbers.
realProblems.errorFeedback: You might assume 'two pieces' automatically means 'two halves', ignoring the segment count. Always count or compare the amount in each piece before deciding if it is truly a half.

realProblems.prompt: A mother has 10 dried beans and wants to share them fairly between her two children so each gets a half of the beans. How many beans should each child receive?
realProblems.answer: Each child should receive 5 beans, since 10 shared equally between two children is 5 and 5 — a fair half each.
realProblems.hint: Share the beans out one at a time, turn by turn, between the two children.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is giving one child a handful first and the other whatever is left, making the shares unequal. Share one bean at a time, alternating between the two children, to keep it fair.

realProblems.prompt: A father buys 2 small buns for his 2 daughters, so each girl gets one whole bun. But he only has 1 large bun left over. Should he give the whole large bun to just one daughter?
realProblems.answer: No — to be fair, the father should cut the large bun into two equal halves and give one half to each daughter, rather than giving the whole bun to only one.
realProblems.hint: When there is one item and two people, cut it into two equal halves to share fairly.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is thinking whoever asks first should get the whole extra item. Fair sharing means splitting into equal halves when there is one item for two people.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A square is cut into one big part and one small part. Explain why this is NOT an example of halves.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: This is not halves because the two parts are not equal — one part is bigger than the other. A half must be one of two EQUAL parts of a whole. Since the square's whole size is shared unfairly between the big part and the small part, neither part can be called a half.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A rectangle is split straight across the middle into two same-size strips. Explain why these two strips ARE halves.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: These two strips are halves because they are exactly the same size — equal parts, not unequal. Since the rectangle is split into exactly two parts and both parts match in size, each strip is one of two equal parts of the whole rectangle, which is what makes it a true half.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how you would draw a line on a square to make sure you create two equal parts, not two unequal parts.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: First fold the square so the two sides land exactly on top of each other — this shows where the middle really is. Then trace a straight line along the fold. Because folding matches the edges exactly, the line always creates two equal parts rather than one bigger part and one smaller part.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Halves Can Be Different Shapes but Equal Size.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Here is a subtle idea worth handling gently. When you fold a square corner to corner, the two halves are triangles — they look different from the halves you get folding straight across, which are rectangles. Yet all of these are still true halves, because each is one of two equal parts. The key message: halves must be equal in size, but they do not have to be the same shape as some other way of halving.
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Fold one square straight across and one square corner to corner. Lay the two triangles on top of each other to show they match — equal. Then talk about how a straight fold gives two rectangle halves and a diagonal fold gives two triangle halves. Both are correct. This prevents the common belief that only one ‘proper’ way of cutting counts as halving.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Two Halves Make a Whole.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The final idea completes the circle: if you put the two halves back together, you get the whole again. This is what makes a half a half — two of them rebuild the original. It also quietly plants the seed that fractions are parts that add back up to one whole, an idea you will meet properly in later years.
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: After cutting a paper shape into two halves, slide them back together to remake the whole. Say the words as they do it: ‘two halves… make one whole’. Play matching games where the child pairs a half-shape with its partner to build a complete shape. The ‘Complete the Other Half’ drawing activity — where you draw the missing half of a butterfly, a house or a face — is another lovely way to feel that two halves make a whole.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in A Whole and Its Parts.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Before you can understand a half, you need the words whole and part. Start with something complete — a whole anjero, a whole mango, a whole biscuit — and name it clearly as ‘the whole’. Then break or cut it and talk about the parts you have made. Keep the language simple and repeat it often across the week.
reasoningPrompts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Hold up a whole anjero. Say, ‘This is the whole anjero.’ Now tear it into two pieces and say, ‘Now I have two parts.’ At this first stage do not worry whether the parts are equal — the aim is simply that the child hears and uses ‘whole’ and ‘part’. Let the child tear their own paper shape and tell you how many parts they made.
